name: Traffic Grid Goal
miniText: The scientific question is whether explicit home-work destinations change congestion relative to undirected circulating traffic. In NetLogo's Traffic Grid Goal model, cars alternate between assigned home and work patches, selecting movement toward their destination while obeying car-following and traffic-light rules. The selected literature connects this mechanism to goal-directed commuting and signal control: the source textbook supplies this concrete destination-based traffic variant [1]; adaptive signal coordination provides a related control mechanism [2]; empirical microscopic traffic states constrain interpretation of congestion patterns [3]. A regular grid and repeated fixed destinations omit heterogeneous schedules and adaptive routing; destination completion is different from simply counting moving cars. The original NetLogo behavior is the baseline for reimplementation. This simulation offers a controlled thought experiment, and agreement with its output does not establish empirical validation.

verification.evidenceSummary: Steering traffic in cities is a very complex task, since improving efficiency involves the coordination of many actors. Traditional approaches attempt to optimize traffic lights for a particular density and configuration of traffic. The disadvantage of this lies in the fact that traffic densities and configurations change constantly. Traffic seems to be an adaptation problem rather than an optimization problem. We propose a simple and feasible alternative, in which traffic lights self-organize to improve traffic flow. We use a multi-agent simulation to study three self-organizing methods, which are able to outperform traditional rigid and adaptive methods. Using simple rules and no direct communication, traffic lights are able to self-organize and adapt to changing traffic conditions, reducing waiting times, number of stopped cars, and increasing average speeds.
